# Vectors in $\reals^n$ {#vectors-in-rn}

Coordinates turn magnitude and direction into algebra

- [One vector has geometric and coordinate descriptions](#one-vector-has-geometric-and-coordinate-descriptions)
- [Vector operations match geometric actions](#vector-operations-match-geometric-actions)
- [The standard basis separates coordinate directions](#the-standard-basis-separates-coordinate-directions)
- [Linear combinations build new directions](#linear-combinations-build-new-directions)
- [Vectors combine physical effects](#vectors-combine-physical-effects)
- [Read geometry from coordinates](#read-geometry-from-coordinates)

## One vector has geometric and coordinate descriptions {#one-vector-has-geometric-and-coordinate-descriptions}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Geometric vector

- directed line segment
- [magnitude]{.alert}: how much
- [direction]{.alert}: which way
- unchanged when translated without rotating or stretching
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Coordinate vector

$$
\vct{v}=\begin{bmatrix}v_1\\v_2\\\vdots\\v_n\end{bmatrix}
\in\reals^n
$$

- ordered list of components
- represented as a column unless stated otherwise
:::
:::

If $P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$ and $Q=(q_1,\ldots,q_n)$, then

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vct{q}-\vct{p}
=\begin{bmatrix}q_1-p_1\\\vdots\\q_n-p_n\end{bmatrix}
$$

## Vector operations match geometric actions {#vector-operations-match-geometric-actions}

For $\vct{u},\vct{v}\in\reals^n$ and $c\in\reals$

$$
\vct{u}+\vct{v}
=\begin{bmatrix}u_1+v_1\\\vdots\\u_n+v_n\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
c\vct{v}
=\begin{bmatrix}cv_1\\\vdots\\cv_n\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Addition

- place vectors head to tail
- parallelogram diagonal
- combine displacements or effects
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Scalar multiplication

- $c>0$: same direction, scaled length
- $c<0$: reversed direction, scaled length
- $c=0$: zero vector
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Coordinate rules preserve the geometric meaning
:::

## The standard basis separates coordinate directions {#the-standard-basis-separates-coordinate-directions}

The $j$th [standard basis vector]{.alert}

$$
\vct{e}_j
=\begin{bmatrix}0&\cdots&0&1&0&\cdots&0\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}
$$

Every coordinate vector decomposes uniquely:

$$
\vct{x}=x_1\vct{e}_1+\cdots+x_n\vct{e}_n
$$

Example in $\reals^3$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\4\end{bmatrix}
=2\vct{e}_1-\vct{e}_2+4\vct{e}_3
$$

::: {.key-point}
Coordinates are the weights of the standard directions
:::

## Linear combinations build new directions {#linear-combinations-build-new-directions}

A [linear combination]{.alert} of $\vct{v}_1,\ldots,\vct{v}_k$ has the form

$$
c_1\vct{v}_1+\cdots+c_k\vct{v}_k
$$

Two nonparallel vectors in $\reals^2$ can build every vector in the plane

Two parallel vectors can build only vectors along one line

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>
Can $\vct{b}=\begin{bmatrix}5\\1\end{bmatrix}$ be built from
$\vct{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\vct{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix}$?

<span class="exsub">Translate the question into one matrix equation</span>
<span class="exsub">Interpret the solution coefficients geometrically</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
This revisits the column view of matrix multiplication. Formal span, linear
independence, basis, and dimension belong to Deck 06.
:::

## Vectors combine physical effects {#vectors-combine-physical-effects}

Two forces act on one object:

$$
\vct{F}_1=\begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}\text{ N},
\qquad
\vct{F}_2=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\end{bmatrix}\text{ N}
$$

Resultant force

$$
\vct{F}=\vct{F}_1+\vct{F}_2
=\begin{bmatrix}2\\6\end{bmatrix}\text{ N}
$$

The components answer algebraic questions; length and direction answer
geometric questions

$$
\norm{\vct{F}}=\sqrt{40}=2\sqrt{10}\text{ N},
\qquad
\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(6,2)
$$

::: {.key-point}
The same vector can be interpreted as displacement, velocity, force, data, or coefficients
:::

## Read geometry from coordinates {#read-geometry-from-coordinates}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>
Let $P=(1,-2,3)$, $Q=(4,0,-1)$, and
$\vct{w}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\-2\end{bmatrix}$

<span class="exsub">Find $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{QP}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Find the endpoint of $\vct{w}$ when its initial point is $P$</span>
<span class="exsub">Express $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ using $\vct{e}_1,\vct{e}_2,\vct{e}_3$</span>
<span class="exsub">Decide whether $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\vct{w}$ are parallel</span>
</span>
:::

# Length, Distance, and Angle

The dot product converts two vectors into geometric information

- [The dot product measures alignment](#the-dot-product-measures-alignment)
- [The norm measures vector length](#the-norm-measures-vector-length)
- [Distance is the length of a difference](#distance-is-the-length-of-a-difference)
- [Cauchy–Schwarz controls every dot product](#cauchy-schwarz-controls-every-dot-product)
- [The dot product determines angle](#the-dot-product-determines-angle)
- [Cosine similarity ignores overall scale](#cosine-similarity-ignores-overall-scale)
- [Compare lengths, distances, and angles](#compare-lengths-distances-and-angles)

## The dot product measures alignment {#the-dot-product-measures-alignment}

Recall the standard dot product on $\reals^n$:

$$
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}
=u_1v_1+\cdots+u_nv_n
$$

It is

- symmetric: $\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}=\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{u}$
- linear in each input
- positive: $\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}\ge0$
- definite: $\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}=0$ only when $\vct{v}=\vct{0}$

For $\vct{u}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\-1\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\vct{v}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}$,

$$
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}=3+0-2=1
$$

::: {.key-point}
Positive dot product — net alignment; negative — net opposition; zero — orthogonality
:::

## The norm measures vector length {#the-norm-measures-vector-length}

The [Euclidean norm]{.alert}

$$
\norm{\vct{v}}
=\sqrt{\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}
=\sqrt{v_1^2+\cdots+v_n^2}
$$

A [unit vector]{.alert} has norm $1$

For $\vct{v}\ne\vct{0}$, normalize without changing direction:

$$
\widehat{\vct{v}}=\frac{\vct{v}}{\norm{\vct{v}}},
\qquad
\norm{\widehat{\vct{v}}}=1
$$

Norm properties

$$
\norm{\vct{v}}\ge0,
\qquad
\norm{c\vct{v}}=\abs{c}\norm{\vct{v}},
\qquad
\norm{\vct{u}+\vct{v}}\le\norm{\vct{u}}+\norm{\vct{v}}
$$

## Distance is the length of a difference {#distance-is-the-length-of-a-difference}

For points represented by $\vct{p},\vct{q}\in\reals^n$

$$
\operatorname{dist}(\vct{p},\vct{q})
=\norm{\vct{q}-\vct{p}}
=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^n(q_j-p_j)^2}
$$

Distance properties

\begin{align*}
\operatorname{dist}(\vct{p},\vct{q})&\ge0
&\text{and equals zero exactly when }\vct{p}=\vct{q}
\\
\operatorname{dist}(\vct{p},\vct{q})&=\operatorname{dist}(\vct{q},\vct{p})
&\text{symmetry}
\\
\operatorname{dist}(\vct{p},\vct{r})
&\le \operatorname{dist}(\vct{p},\vct{q})
+\operatorname{dist}(\vct{q},\vct{r})
&\text{triangle inequality}
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
Subtract points to obtain a displacement vector; measure its norm to obtain distance
:::

## Cauchy–Schwarz controls every dot product {#cauchy-schwarz-controls-every-dot-product}

For all $\vct{u},\vct{v}\in\reals^n$,

$$
\abs{\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}
\le \norm{\vct{u}}\norm{\vct{v}}
$$

Equality holds exactly when $\vct{u}$ and $\vct{v}$ are linearly dependent

Why the bound matters:

$$
-1\le
\frac{\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}
{\norm{\vct{u}}\norm{\vct{v}}}
\le1
\qquad
(\vct{u},\vct{v}\ne\vct{0})
$$

::: {.key-point}
[Cauchy–Schwarz]{.alert} makes the angle formula possible in every $\reals^n$
:::

::: {.notes}
One proof considers the nonnegative quadratic
$\norm{\vct{u}-t\vct{v}}^2$ and requires its discriminant to be nonpositive.
Develop that proof at the board if time permits.
:::

## The dot product determines angle {#the-dot-product-determines-angle}

For nonzero vectors, define $0\le\theta\le\pi$ by

$$
\cos\theta
=\frac{\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}
{\norm{\vct{u}}\norm{\vct{v}}}
$$

| Dot product | Angle | Geometry |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| $>0$ | $0\le\theta<\pi/2$ | acute; aligned |
| $=0$ | $\theta=\pi/2$ | orthogonal |
| $<0$ | $\pi/2<\theta\le\pi$ | obtuse; opposed |

For unit vectors $\widehat{\vct{u}}$ and $\widehat{\vct{v}}$,

$$
\widehat{\vct{u}}^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\vct{v}}=\cos\theta
$$

## Cosine similarity ignores overall scale {#cosine-similarity-ignores-overall-scale}

For nonzero data vectors

$$
\operatorname{cosim}(\vct{x},\vct{y})
=\frac{\vct{x}^{\mathsf T}\vct{y}}
{\norm{\vct{x}}\norm{\vct{y}}}
$$

- near $1$: similar direction
- near $0$: weak directional relationship
- near $-1$: opposite direction

Multiplying either vector by a positive scalar leaves cosine similarity unchanged

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Useful when

- direction or profile matters
- overall magnitude should be ignored
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Not enough when

- absolute size matters
- offsets or unequal feature scales distort meaning
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Geometry supplies a model; the application decides whether it is appropriate
:::

## Compare lengths, distances, and angles {#compare-lengths-distances-and-angles}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>
Let $\vct{u}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{bmatrix}$ and
$\vct{v}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{bmatrix}$

<span class="exsub">Find $\norm{\vct{u}}$, $\norm{\vct{v}}$, and $\norm{\vct{u}-\vct{v}}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Find the angle between $\vct{u}$ and $\vct{v}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Verify Cauchy–Schwarz numerically</span>
<span class="exsub">Explain which computation measures point separation and which measures directional similarity</span>
</span>
:::

# Orthogonality and Projection

Split a vector into a chosen direction and a perpendicular residual

- [Orthogonality makes lengths add by squares](#orthogonality-makes-lengths-add-by-squares)
- [Projection extracts one directional component](#projection-extracts-one-directional-component)
- [Projection produces an orthogonal decomposition](#projection-produces-an-orthogonal-decomposition)
- [The residual gives distance to a line](#the-residual-gives-distance-to-a-line)
- [A projection is a matrix transformation](#a-projection-is-a-matrix-transformation)
- [Complementary projections split every vector](#complementary-projections-split-every-vector)
- [Decompose a vector](#decompose-a-vector)

## Orthogonality makes lengths add by squares {#orthogonality-makes-lengths-add-by-squares}

Vectors $\vct{u}$ and $\vct{v}$ are [orthogonal]{.alert} when

$$
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}=0
$$

Then

\begin{align*}
\norm{\vct{u}+\vct{v}}^2
&=(\vct{u}+\vct{v})^{\mathsf T}(\vct{u}+\vct{v})\\
&=\norm{\vct{u}}^2+2\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}+\norm{\vct{v}}^2\\
&=\norm{\vct{u}}^2+\norm{\vct{v}}^2
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
The Pythagorean theorem is a dot-product identity
:::

## Projection extracts one directional component {#projection-extracts-one-directional-component}

Let $\vct{v}\ne\vct{0}$

The [scalar component]{.alert} of $\vct{u}$ along $\vct{v}$ is

$$
\operatorname{comp}_{\vct{v}}\vct{u}
=\frac{\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}{\norm{\vct{v}}}
$$

The [vector projection]{.alert} is

$$
\operatorname{proj}_{\vct{v}}\vct{u}
=\frac{\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}
{\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}\vct{v}
$$

If $\widehat{\vct{v}}=\vct{v}/\norm{\vct{v}}$, then

$$
\operatorname{proj}_{\vct{v}}\vct{u}
=(\widehat{\vct{v}}^{\mathsf T}\vct{u})\widehat{\vct{v}}
$$

## Projection produces an orthogonal decomposition {#projection-produces-an-orthogonal-decomposition}

Write

$$
\vct{u}=\underbrace{\operatorname{proj}_{\vct{v}}\vct{u}}_{\text{parallel to }\vct{v}}
+\underbrace{\vct{r}}_{\text{orthogonal to }\vct{v}}
$$

where

$$
\vct{r}=\vct{u}-\operatorname{proj}_{\vct{v}}\vct{u}
$$

Check orthogonality:

\begin{align*}
\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{r}
&=\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{u}
-\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}
\left(\frac{\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}
{\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}\vct{v}\right)\\
&=0
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
Projection chooses the unique point on the line through $\vct{v}$ with a perpendicular residual
:::

## The residual gives distance to a line {#the-residual-gives-distance-to-a-line}

Line through $\vct{x}_0$ with direction $\vct{v}\ne\vct{0}$:

$$
L=\{\vct{x}_0+t\vct{v}:t\in\reals\}
$$

From point $\vct{p}$, first form the displacement $\vct{p}-\vct{x}_0$

Nearest point on the line

$$
\vct{x}_*=\vct{x}_0
+\operatorname{proj}_{\vct{v}}(\vct{p}-\vct{x}_0)
$$

Distance to the line

$$
\operatorname{dist}(\vct{p},L)
=\norm{\vct{p}-\vct{x}_*}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Nearest means [perpendicular residual]{.alert}
:::

## A projection is a matrix transformation {#a-projection-is-a-matrix-transformation}

For a unit vector $\vct{q}$, projection onto its line is

$$
\operatorname{proj}_{\vct{q}}\vct{x}
=(\vct{q}^{\mathsf T}\vct{x})\vct{q}
=\underbrace{\vct{q}\vct{q}^{\mathsf T}}_{\mat{P}}\vct{x}
$$

The projection matrix

$$
\mat{P}=\vct{q}\vct{q}^{\mathsf T}
$$

satisfies

$$
\mat{P}^{\mathsf T}=\mat{P},
\qquad
\mat{P}^2=\mat{P}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Symmetric — the geometry is orthogonal<br>
Idempotent — projecting twice changes nothing
:::

## Complementary projections split every vector {#complementary-projections-split-every-vector}

Projection onto the line through unit $\vct{q}$:

$$
\mat{P}=\vct{q}\vct{q}^{\mathsf T}
$$

Projection onto the perpendicular hyperplane:

$$
\mat{Q}=\mat{I}-\mat{P}
$$

Every $\vct{x}$ splits as

$$
\vct{x}=\mat{P}\vct{x}+\mat{Q}\vct{x},
\qquad
(\mat{P}\vct{x})^{\mathsf T}(\mat{Q}\vct{x})=0
$$

and therefore

$$
\norm{\vct{x}}^2
=\norm{\mat{P}\vct{x}}^2+\norm{\mat{Q}\vct{x}}^2
$$

::: {.notes}
Deck 03 constructed the plane projection $\mat{Q}=\mat{I}-\vct{q}\vct{q}^{\mathsf T}$
from a unit normal vector. Here it appears as one half of a complementary pair.
:::

# Geometry of Linear Systems

Equations, parameters, and vectors describe the same solution set

- [A line is a point plus one direction](#a-line-is-a-point-plus-one-direction)
- [A plane has parametric and normal descriptions](#a-plane-has-parametric-and-normal-descriptions)
- [A normal vector converts geometry into an equation](#a-normal-vector-converts-geometry-into-an-equation)
- [A linear system intersects hyperplanes](#a-linear-system-intersects-hyperplanes)
- [Every consistent solution set is a translate](#every-consistent-solution-set-is-a-translate)
- [Pivots and free variables predict geometry](#pivots-and-free-variables-predict-geometry)
- [Translate elimination into geometry](#translate-elimination-into-geometry)

## A line is a point plus one direction {#a-line-is-a-point-plus-one-direction}

A line through $\vct{x}_0\in\reals^n$ parallel to
$\vct{v}\ne\vct{0}$:

$$
\vct{x}=\vct{x}_0+t\vct{v},
\qquad t\in\reals
$$

In $\reals^3$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{bmatrix}
+t\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{bmatrix}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
x=1+2t,
\qquad y=-2+t,
\qquad z=3-t
$$

::: {.key-point}
Point $+$ parameter $\times$ direction
:::

## A plane has parametric and normal descriptions {#a-plane-has-parametric-and-normal-descriptions}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Two directions

For nonparallel $\vct{v},\vct{w}\in\reals^3$

$$
\vct{x}=\vct{x}_0+s\vct{v}+t\vct{w}
$$

$s,t\in\reals$
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### One normal

For $\vct{n}\ne\vct{0}$ perpendicular to the plane

$$
\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{x}-\vct{x}_0)=0
$$

equivalently $\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}\vct{x}=b$
:::
:::

The descriptions agree when

$$
\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}=0,
\qquad
\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}\vct{w}=0,
\qquad
b=\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}\vct{x}_0
$$

## A normal vector converts geometry into an equation {#a-normal-vector-converts-geometry-into-an-equation}

Plane through $\vct{x}_0=(1,0,2)$ with normal
$\vct{n}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{bmatrix}$

Point-normal form

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&3\end{bmatrix}
\left(
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix}
-\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}
\right)=0
$$

Coordinate form

$$
2(x-1)-y+3(z-2)=0
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
2x-y+3z=8
$$

Distance from $\vct{p}$ to the plane

$$
\operatorname{dist}(\vct{p},H)
=\frac{\abs{\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}\vct{p}-b}}{\norm{\vct{n}}}
$$

## A linear system intersects hyperplanes {#a-linear-system-intersects-hyperplanes}

Write the rows of $\mat{A}$ as $\vct{a}_1^{\mathsf T},\ldots,
\vct{a}_m^{\mathsf T}$:

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\vct{a}_i^{\mathsf T}\vct{x}=b_i,
\quad i=1,\ldots,m
$$

Each equation describes a hyperplane with normal $\vct{a}_i$

The solution set is their intersection:

- one point — unique solution
- a line, plane, or higher-dimensional flat — infinitely many solutions
- empty intersection — inconsistent system

::: {.key-point}
Elimination finds the intersection; geometry explains its shape
:::

## Every consistent solution set is a translate {#every-consistent-solution-set-is-a-translate}

Suppose $\vct{x}_p$ is one particular solution of
$\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$

Every other solution has the form

$$
\vct{x}=\vct{x}_p+\vct{z},
\qquad
\mat{A}\vct{z}=\vct{0}
$$

because

$$
\mat{A}(\vct{x}_p+\vct{z})
=\mat{A}\vct{x}_p+\mat{A}\vct{z}
=\vct{b}
$$

Conversely, the difference of any two solutions satisfies the homogeneous system

::: {.key-point}
Consistent solution set $=$ one particular point $+$ all homogeneous directions
:::

::: {.notes}
Deck 06 will name the homogeneous directions the null space and explain why
they form a subspace.
:::

## Pivots and free variables predict geometry {#pivots-and-free-variables-predict-geometry}

For a consistent system with $n$ unknowns

| Free variables | Typical solution geometry in $\reals^n$ |
|:---:|:---|
| $0$ | one point |
| $1$ | line |
| $2$ | plane |
| $k$ | $k$-parameter flat |

If there are $r$ pivot variables, then there are

$$
n-r
$$

free variables

::: {.key-point}
The number of free parameters is the dimension of the solution directions
:::

::: {.notes}
State this as geometric preview. Rank, nullity, and the fundamental spaces are
developed formally in Deck 06.
:::

## Translate elimination into geometry {#translate-elimination-into-geometry}

Consider

\begin{align*}
x+y+z&=2\\
x-y+z&=0
\end{align*}

Elimination gives $y=1$ and $x+z=1$

$$
\vct{x}
=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}
+t\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The direction vector is perpendicular to both row normals:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}
\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}=0,
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}
\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}=0
$$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>
Explain why the intersection of the two planes is parallel to this direction
</span>
:::

# Cross Products and Orientation

In $\reals^3$, two directions determine a perpendicular direction and an area

- [The cross product produces a perpendicular vector](#the-cross-product-produces-a-perpendicular-vector)
- [Order determines orientation](#order-determines-orientation)
- [Cross-product magnitude is parallelogram area](#cross-product-magnitude-is-parallelogram-area)
- [The scalar triple product is signed volume](#the-scalar-triple-product-is-signed-volume)
- [Cross products build plane normals](#cross-products-build-plane-normals)
- [Torque combines leverage and force](#torque-combines-leverage-and-force)
- [Use the cross product geometrically](#use-the-cross-product-geometrically)

## The cross product produces a perpendicular vector {#the-cross-product-produces-a-perpendicular-vector}

For $\vct{u},\vct{v}\in\reals^3$

$$
\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}
=\begin{bmatrix}
u_2v_3-u_3v_2\\
u_3v_1-u_1v_3\\
u_1v_2-u_2v_1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Its defining geometry:

$$
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v})=0,
\qquad
\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v})=0
$$

For $\vct{e}_1$ and $\vct{e}_2$,

$$
\vct{e}_1\mathbin{\times}\vct{e}_2=\vct{e}_3
$$

::: {.key-point}
Two input vectors in $\reals^3$ produce a vector perpendicular to both
:::

## Order determines orientation {#order-determines-orientation}

The cross product is [not commutative]{.alert}:

$$
\vct{v}\mathbin{\times}\vct{u}
=-(\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v})
$$

Right-hand rule

- curl fingers from $\vct{u}$ toward $\vct{v}$ through the smaller angle
- thumb points along $\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}$

Cyclic standard-basis products

$$
\vct{e}_1\mathbin{\times}\vct{e}_2=\vct{e}_3,
\qquad
\vct{e}_2\mathbin{\times}\vct{e}_3=\vct{e}_1,
\qquad
\vct{e}_3\mathbin{\times}\vct{e}_1=\vct{e}_2
$$

Reverse either order to reverse the sign

## Cross-product magnitude is parallelogram area {#cross-product-magnitude-is-parallelogram-area}

If $\theta$ is the angle between $\vct{u}$ and $\vct{v}$, then

$$
\norm{\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}}
=\norm{\vct{u}}\norm{\vct{v}}\sin\theta
$$

Base times perpendicular height

$$
\underbrace{\norm{\vct{u}}}_{\text{base}}
\underbrace{\norm{\vct{v}}\sin\theta}_{\text{height}}
$$

Triangle area

$$
\frac12\norm{\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}}
$$

The area is zero exactly when the vectors are parallel or one is zero

::: {.key-point}
Dot product measures alignment; cross-product magnitude measures perpendicular spread
:::

## The scalar triple product is signed volume {#the-scalar-triple-product-is-signed-volume}

For $\vct{u},\vct{v},\vct{w}\in\reals^3$

$$
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{v}\mathbin{\times}\vct{w})
=\det\begin{bmatrix}\vct{u}&\vct{v}&\vct{w}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Absolute value — volume of the parallelepiped

Sign — orientation of the ordered triple

Zero — the three vectors lie in one plane

::: {.key-point}
The cross product reconnects Chapter 3 geometry to the determinant
:::

## Cross products build plane normals {#cross-products-build-plane-normals}

Three noncollinear points $P,Q,R\in\reals^3$ determine a plane

Two directions in the plane:

$$
\vct{u}=\overrightarrow{PQ},
\qquad
\vct{v}=\overrightarrow{PR}
$$

A normal vector:

$$
\vct{n}=\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}
$$

Plane equation:

$$
\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{x}-\vct{p})=0
$$

::: {.key-point}
Two in-plane directions $\longrightarrow$ one perpendicular normal $\longrightarrow$ one plane equation
:::

## Torque combines leverage and force {#torque-combines-leverage-and-force}

Force $\vct{F}$ applied at position $\vct{r}$ relative to a pivot produces torque

$$
\vct{\tau}=\vct{r}\mathbin{\times}\vct{F}
$$

Magnitude

$$
\norm{\vct{\tau}}
=\norm{\vct{r}}\norm{\vct{F}}\sin\theta
$$

- only the component of force perpendicular to the lever arm turns the object
- direction gives the rotation axis by the right-hand rule
- zero torque when force acts along the lever arm

::: {.key-point}
Cross products package size and oriented perpendicular direction together
:::

## Use the cross product geometrically {#use-the-cross-product-geometrically}

</span>
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- A vector in $\reals^n$ is both a [coordinate object and a geometric direction]{.alert}
- Dot products create length, distance, angle, and orthogonality
- Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality guarantee that these measurements behave geometrically
- Projection splits a vector into [parallel and perpendicular components]{.alert}; the residual measures nearest-point error
- A consistent linear system describes one particular point plus all homogeneous directions
- In $\reals^3$, the cross product supplies an oriented perpendicular direction, area, plane normals, and volume

# What Comes Next

Euclidean geometry gave concrete meaning to vectors in $\reals^n$

[General Vector Spaces]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}) will keep the algebraic rules while allowing new kinds of vectors:

- polynomials
- functions
- matrices
- solution sets of homogeneous systems
